about: Which numeric datatypes each accelerator ARCHITECTURE accepts as a compute operand. VENDOR-PUBLISHED CAPABILITY FACTS ONLY -- this file records SUPPORT (a documented capability), never PERFORMANCE: no TOPS/TFLOPS, no clocks, no measured rates, no machine inventory. Rows are architectures, not products or machines. Consumed by the dtype-bits page's hardware-support view.
unknown_rule: `unknown` means the vendor does not publish the answer. It is a DISTINCT state from `none` and must render as unknown -- never collapse it to a guess, a default, or a `none`. `none` is used only where a vendor enumerates a complete operand list that omits the dtype, or where the architecture has no engine that could accept it. A vendor's TOOLCHAIN accepting a dtype is not the same claim as its ENGINE multiplying in that dtype; where a vendor's own documents blur the two, the note says which one the level records.

levels.native: Documented native operand of the architecture's MATRIX / tensor engine.
levels.vector: Documented native operand of the vector / SIMD / scalar ALU only -- there is no matrix engine, or the matrix engine does not take this dtype.
levels.emulated: Reachable only by converting (upconverting / decompressing) to a wider type the hardware does accept.
levels.none: Documented as not supported by this architecture -- including the common case where a vendor toolchain ACCEPTS a wider dtype and then executes it at a narrower one (fp32 in, fp16 math): the engine has no path for it. `emulated` is the opposite direction, a narrow dtype WIDENED to something the hardware accepts.
levels.unknown: Not publicly documented by the vendor.

classes.gpu-matrix: GPU with a dedicated matrix/tensor engine (Tensor Core, WMMA, XMX/DPAS).
classes.gpu-alu: GPU with no matrix engine -- GEMM is emitted as vector/scalar FMA and integer dot products.
classes.npu: Fixed-function neural accelerator or AI ASIC.
classes.dsp: Audio/vector DSP core used for on-device inference.
classes.cpu-simd: CPU SIMD/vector ISA path (and, where present, a CPU tile-matrix unit).

architectures.source: NVIDIA CUDA Programming Guide, Table 33 "Input Data Types Supported by Tensor Core Acceleration per Compute Capability" (CC 12.x) + CUDA PTX ISA `mma` + the RTX Blackwell architecture whitepaper

fp32.note: CUDA-core FMA operand and the Tensor Core ACCUMULATOR type; TF32 is the 32-bit-range format the tensor engine actually ingests.

fp8e4m3.note: OCP FP8; also the element type inside the NVFP4/MXFP8 block-scaled forms.

int4.note: INT4 tensor-core mma existed on Turing-Ada (sm_75-sm_89) and is gone here: the CUDA guide's per-compute-capability input-dtype table lists INT4 only through CC 8.9, and the sub-byte WMMA API is documented as "deprecated and will be removed in sm_90". Sub-byte moved to the FP4/FP6 block-scaled float formats instead.

architectures.source: AMD "RDNA 4" Instruction Set Architecture Reference Guide (WMMA operand table)

fp32.note: fp32 is the WMMA ACCUMULATOR, never an A/B multiplicand on this generation -- fp32 multiply happens on the vector ALU.

fp16.note: V_WMMA_F32_16X16X16_F16 and the F16-accumulate form.

fp8e4m3.note: AMD spells e4m3 "FP8"; four WMMA forms cover every FP8/BF8 pairing of the two operands.

int8.note: One instruction serves signed and unsigned (AMD's "IU8" naming), accumulating into int32.

int4.note: Two int4 matrix forms, one of them double-K, plus sparse variants -- 4-bit is a first-class matrix-core operand here, not a curiosity. Very few engines can say that.

architectures.source: AMD "RDNA 2" Instruction Set Architecture Reference Guide (VOP3P dot-product opcodes)

fp16.note: Packed fp16 FMA in the vector ALU -- there is no matrix engine on this generation.

bf16.note: The RDNA 2 ISA guide is a complete opcode reference and contains no bf16 operand anywhere -- bf16 reaches AMD consumer GPUs one generation later.

int8.note: A 4-wide int8 dot product into an int32 accumulator, on the vector ALU -- AMD's stated purpose is inference. No matrix engine exists on this generation.

int4.note: AMD's own description is "dot product of signed nibbles": an 8-wide int4 dot into int32. Real 4-bit arithmetic without a matrix engine -- which is exactly why `vector` and `native` are separate levels here.

fp32.note: DPAS accumulates in fp32; TF32 is the 32-bit-range matrix operand.

fp16.note: `intel_sub_group_f16_f16_matrix_mad_k16`.

fp8e4m3.note: No Intel specification lists FP8 as an XMX operand for this generation: the OpenCL, SPIR-V and SYCL matrix extensions define fp16 / bf16 / tf32 / int8 / int4 and no e4m3 or e5m2 stem. FP8 weights are dequantized to a documented operand type before they reach the systolic array.

fp8e5m2.note: No Intel specification lists FP8 as an XMX operand for this generation: the OpenCL, SPIR-V and SYCL matrix extensions define fp16 / bf16 / tf32 / int8 / int4 and no e4m3 or e5m2 stem. FP8 weights are dequantized to a documented operand type before they reach the systolic array.

int8.note: `intel_sub_group_i8_i8_matrix_mad_k32`, K=32 per step.

int4.note: Intel's XMX OpenCL extension defines i4/u4 (and mixed i8xi4) matrix-mad stems at K=64 -- the sub-byte weight path. Intel publishes that operand list per extension rather than per architecture, and a device reports at runtime which stems it implements.

architectures.source: Apple coremltools documentation -- "Typed Execution" and "Quantization Overview"

fp32.note: Apple bars the Neural Engine outright for a model typed fp32; the work falls back to CPU/GPU.

fp16.note: "The GPU and NE use float 16 precision."

int8.note: Apple documents int8 activations AND weights reaching optimized Neural Engine compute on its newer chips.

architectures.source: Tenstorrent's published Tensix ISA documentation (matrix-unit source registers + float bit patterns)

fp32.note: The matrix unit's source registers hold at most 19 bits: fp32 appears only as a DESTINATION accumulator and as a vector-unit format, never as a matrix operand.

fp16.note: An fp16 x fp16 source pair accumulating into fp32 or fp16 -- though the user-facing tensor API exposes bf16 rather than fp16.

bf16.note: bf16 (and tf32) are the documented float source formats for the matrix unit.

fp8e4m3.note: The published operand table has no fp8 at all; the open runtime converts an e4m3 tensor to a 16-bit float format on its way to the engine.

fp8e5m2.note: The format enum spans several hardware generations and carries fp8-family entries whose layouts are not published, so this generation's answer is not documented.

int8.note: An int8 x int8 source pair accumulating into int32.

int4.note: Not a matrix operand. Tenstorrent's sub-byte formats are BLOCK FLOAT (a shared exponent across a block of values, 4 or 2 bits of magnitude each), which the unpacker expands into 16-bit-shaped source registers before the engine sees them -- a different idea from an int4 operand, and one this page's seven columns cannot express.

architectures.source: Cadence Tensilica HiFi DSP family datasheet + the per-core HiFi product specifications

fp32.note: Floating point is an OPTIONAL unit on this core -- a licensee can ship it without one, in which case the DSP is fixed-point only.

fp16.note: Half-precision floating point appears one generation later; HiFi 4's optional FPU is single-precision.

bf16.note: Cadence enumerates MAC widths and an optional FPU, never a closed list of floating-point formats, so bf16 is unaddressed rather than excluded.

fp8e4m3.note: No published operand list for fp8 to be present in or absent from.

fp8e5m2.note: No published operand list for fp8 to be present in or absent from.

int8.note: The published MAC widths stop at 16x16 -- 8-bit data is widened into a 16-bit multiply. Cadence's own HiFi 4 neural-network library declares the 4-bit entry points and ships them as stubs that return an error, while the next generation implements them for real.

int4.note: See int8: not a MAC operand on this core.

architectures.source: Cadence Tensilica HiFi DSP family datasheet + the per-core HiFi product specifications

fp32.note: Optional single-precision floating-point MACs -- floating point is a licensing choice on these DSPs, not a given.

fp16.note: Optional half-precision floating-point MACs, at twice the single-precision rate.

bf16.note: Cadence enumerates MAC widths and an optional FPU, never a closed list of floating-point formats, so bf16 is unaddressed rather than excluded.

fp8e4m3.note: No published operand list for fp8 to be present in or absent from.

fp8e5m2.note: No published operand list for fp8 to be present in or absent from.

architectures.source: Intel 64 and IA-32 Architectures Software Developer's Manual, Vol. 2 (instruction set reference)

fp32.note: VFMADD -- the baseline vector FMA.

fp16.note: F16C is defined as 16-bit floating-point CONVERSION only: you unpack fp16 to fp32, compute, and pack back. Real fp16 arithmetic does not exist on x86 until AVX512-FP16.

int8.note: VPMADDUBSW multiplies unsigned by signed bytes into 16-bit intermediates -- real 8-bit multipliers. What VNNI adds later is the fused 4-wide accumulate into int32.

int4.note: x86 SIMD element sizes are 8/16/32/64-bit; there is no 4-bit operand.

architectures.source: Intel Architecture Instruction Set Extensions Programming Reference (AVX512_VNNI, AVX512_BF16, AVX512_FP16)

fp16.note: AVX512-FP16 adds real half-precision arithmetic; without that extension fp16 is convert-only.

bf16.note: VDPBF16PS -- a bf16 pair dot-product into fp32. Convert-and-dot, not full bf16 arithmetic.

int8.note: VPDPBUSD: a 4-wide u8 x s8 dot product into an int32 accumulator -- the instruction the whole int8 CPU path is built on. Base VNNI is mixed-signedness only; a later AVX-VNNI-INT8 extension adds the s8xs8, u8xu8 and u8xs8 forms.

int4.note: int4 weights on a CPU are unpacked to int8 in registers first.

architectures.source: Intel Architecture Instruction Set Extensions and Future Features Programming Reference (AMX-INT8 / AMX-BF16 / AMX-FP16 / AMX-FP8, enumerated in CPUID.1EH.01H:EAX)

fp32.note: Tiles accumulate INTO fp32, but fp32 is not a tile operand.

fp16.note: AMX-FP16 -- a later addition than the original INT8/BF16 pair.

bf16.note: AMX-BF16, in the first AMX generation.

fp8e4m3.note: AMX-FP8 (the TDP*F8PS family) takes E5M2 and E4M3 tiles -- including mixed E5M2xE4M3 -- and always accumulates into fp32. It is enumerated separately from the original INT8/BF16 pair and arrives in a later AMX generation.

fp8e5m2.note: AMX-FP8 (the TDP*F8PS family) takes E5M2 and E4M3 tiles -- including mixed E5M2xE4M3 -- and always accumulates into fp32. It is enumerated separately from the original INT8/BF16 pair and arrives in a later AMX generation.

int8.note: AMX-INT8 -- a genuine matrix engine inside a CPU core, which is why this row reads like a GPU row.

architectures.source: Arm Architecture Reference Manual for A-profile

fp16.note: Half-precision ARITHMETIC is gated behind a separate architecture feature; baseline NEON only converts fp16 to fp32 and back.

int8.note: Widening multiply-accumulate (SMLAL) -- no dot-product instruction yet.

int4.note: Advanced SIMD element sizes are 8/16/32/64-bit, so no 4-bit operand exists -- Arm never writes a sentence denying int4, the element-size table is simply closed.

architectures.source: Arm Architecture Reference Manual for A-profile (FEAT_FP16, FEAT_DotProd)

fp16.note: FEAT_FP16 makes half-precision a real arithmetic type.

int8.note: SDOT/UDOT: 4-wide int8 dot into an int32 lane -- the Arm counterpart of VNNI and DP4A.

architectures.source: Arm Architecture Reference Manual for A-profile (FEAT_I8MM, FEAT_BF16)

fp32.note: fp32 is the accumulator for every NEON matrix instruction, never a multiplicand: fp32 matrix multiply exists only in SVE, not in Advanced SIMD, at any feature level.

bf16.note: BFMMLA multiplies a 2x4 by a 4x2 bf16 block into a 2x2 fp32 accumulator -- a matrix instruction on a CPU. BFDOT gives the same operand type a plain 2-wide dot into fp32.

fp8e4m3.note: FP8 reaches the A-profile architecture later (Armv9.2), as its own feature set with its own matrix instructions.

fp8e5m2.note: See e4m3: a later architecture revision, not this feature set.

int8.note: SMMLA/UMMLA multiply a 2x8 by an 8x2 int8 block into a 2x2 int32 accumulator -- equivalent to an 8-way dot product per destination element.
